planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or sow in early spring after a moist chilling period, into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: European goldenrod is the goldenrod species native to Europe and temperate Asia, the original plant from which the genus Solidago takes its name, long predating the American species now common in gardens. Compared to many taller North American relatives it forms a modest, well-mannered clump of basal rosette leaves topped by slender wandlike stems bearing tight clusters of small golden-yellow flowers from late summer into fall. It adapts readily to sandy, rocky, or average garden loam and shrugs off both drought and occasional wet spells once established, needing no fertilizer or staking. Because it self-sows freely in favorable sites, deadhead spent flower clusters before seed drop if you want to keep its spread contained within a bed.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification into dry to average, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants spread by shallow rhizomes to form loose colonies.

directions: Missouri goldenrod is a shorter, colony-forming prairie native ranging from the Rocky Mountain foothills east through the Great Plains and upper Midwest, its smooth reddish stems and narrow leaves setting it apart from taller, rougher-textured goldenrods sharing its range. It spreads by shallow rhizomes into loose, manageable colonies rather than dense stands, making it well suited to dry prairie restorations and mixed native borders. Flat-topped clusters of bright yellow flowers open in mid to late summer, earlier than many other goldenrod species, extending the nectar season for prairie bees and butterflies. It thrives in dry, well-drained soils including sand and gravel with no irrigation or feeding once established, though it can struggle in heavy, poorly drained clay.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification into sharply drained, dry to average soil, including alkaline sites, in full sun.

directions: Baby goldenrod, also called dwarf goldenrod, is one of the shortest species in the genus, forming low rhizomatous colonies across dry meadows, alkaline flats, and open slopes of the intermountain West and central Rockies. Its compact stature makes it far better suited to rock gardens, xeric borders, and alpine-style plantings than the taller, more sprawling goldenrods commonly grown in eastern gardens. Slender, plume-like clusters of small golden flowers appear atop wiry stems in mid to late summer, drawing native bees during a season when many other nectar sources have already faded. It requires sharply drained soil and full sun, tolerating alkaline conditions and drought far better than wet or overly rich garden ground.
sources: Idaho Fish and Game Species Catalog

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this species needs sustained soil moisture and will not tolerate a dry site.

directions: Roundleaf goldenrod, also known as swamp goldenrod, is one of the few goldenrods truly adapted to shaded wetlands, occurring naturally in forested swamps, fens, and the wooded margins of streams and lakes across the eastern United States. Its large, rough-textured, rounded basal leaves are noticeably broader than those of most other goldenrods and taper into long winged petioles, giving the plant a bold, coarse presence at the base well before the flowering stems rise. In late summer it sends up a broad, open, dome-shaped panicle of small yellow flowers held well above the foliage, drawing late-season pollinators into shaded wetland plantings where few other goldenrods will grow. Site it in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where its spreading rhizomatous roots also help stabilize streambanks and shorelines.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

common_name: Climax Aster (Tall Pale Blue New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Climax is a tall, sturdy heirloom selection that benefits from staking or underplanting to hide its lower stems.

directions: Climax is a long-cultivated, tall-growing New York aster selection prized for its unusually large, pale lavender-blue single flowers, which open in great numbers atop stout, upright stems well above the surrounding foliage in early to mid fall. Its height and vigor make it a back-of-border anchor rather than a front-row plant, pairing well with ornamental grasses and other late-season perennials that can support its stems. The blooms attract abundant bees and late-migrating butterflies at a time when few other tall perennials are still flowering. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to renew vigor, maintain flower size, and keep the planting from thinning out in the center.

common_name: Lady in Black Aster (Dark-Leaved Calico Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lady in Black holds its dark foliage color best with some direct sun.

directions: Lady in Black is a selection of the native calico aster grown as much for its foliage as its flowers, emerging in deep purple-black tones that persist through summer heat before fading only slightly by fall. Airy, horizontally branched sprays of tiny white, pink-centered daisies smother the dark stems in late summer and autumn, creating a striking two-tone effect against the near-black leaves. It tolerates dry shade and part-sun conditions better than most garden asters, making it a useful dark-foliage accent for woodland edges and mixed borders alike. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous, well-colored new growth and control its naturally spreading habit.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center plant trial notes

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; shining aster spreads by creeping rhizomes and is best suited to wet meadows, pond edges, and rain gardens.

directions: Shining aster takes its common name from the glossy, narrow, clasping leaves that line its stout stems, a feature that helps distinguish it from other tall wetland asters even before it flowers. It grows from long creeping rhizomes into substantial colonies in moist to wet meadows, marsh edges, and streambanks, sending up erect, purple-streaked stems topped with an open spray of pale violet to nearly white flowers from late summer into October. The extended three-month bloom window makes it an outstanding late-season nectar source, drawing a wide range of bee species as well as migrating butterflies to wet garden sites. Give it consistently moist to wet soil and full sun to partial shade, and allow room for its rhizomes to spread when planting rain gardens or pond margins.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this woodland-edge species forms an evergreen basal rosette that stays attractive through winter.

directions: White arrowleaf aster is named for its distinctive arrow-shaped upper leaves, broadly winged at the petiole, which set it apart from other woodland-edge asters even before the flowers appear. It forms a semi-evergreen rosette of basal leaves that persists through much of winter, then sends up branching stems bearing a dense, pyramidal spray of small white, yellow-centered flowers from late summer into October. Found naturally along the margins of moist to dry forests, fields, and roadbanks across the eastern and midwestern United States, it tolerates more shade than many garden asters while still flowering reliably. The abundant small blooms support a wide range of bees and flies and serve as a larval host for the Pearl Crescent butterfly, making it a useful addition to woodland edges and naturalized plantings.
